title: Textbooks Don't Have to Be This Bad
author: Michael Pershan
summary: Michael Pershan adapts the worked-example research underlying his book Teaching Math With Examples into two concrete recommendations for textbook design, publishing the piece first for the Chartered Institute of Editing and Proofreading and cross-posting it to his own newsletter. He opens with a personal anecdote about a bright, well-illustrated meteorology textbook that nonetheless overwhelmed him within minutes, using it to argue that attractive design isn't the same as learnable design. His first recommendation is to ask more questions more often within the body of the text itself, since studying a textbook is a form of direct instruction that risks leaving students in surface-level comprehension without a teacher present to check understanding in real time. His second recommendation draws on Mayer and Moreno's cognitive-load research, offering four specific techniques for structuring dense material into manageable chunks: cutting extraneous content, previewing structure before detail, segmenting long explanations, and aligning text tightly with its illustrations. Pershan is explicit that he isn't proposing a science of textbook design, only a research-informed art, and frames the whole piece as advocacy for incremental improvement over grand reinvention. He closes by inviting readers to try the exercise themselves: find a difficult textbook passage, break it into its component steps, and rewrite it using the structure-then-detail approach.
points: Pershan applies the worked-example research behind his book Teaching Math With Examples to textbook design generally, arguing textbooks are a form of direct instruction with the teacher missing and need the same scaffolding a good live explanation would provide.
His first recommendation - ask more questions, more often, woven directly into the text - targets the surface-level comprehension problem where students read fluently but retain little.

His second recommendation draws on Mayer and Moreno's cognitive-load research, offering four concrete techniques (cut extraneous content, preview the structure, segment complexity, align text with illustrations) for reducing overload in dense material.

He frames the piece as intentionally modest - tiny improvements to existing textbook design rather than a reimagining of the format - positioning incremental, research-informed tweaks as more valuable than sweeping vision statements.
quotes: I recently opened the latest edition of a college-level meteorology textbook. Each page, I happily discovered, was colourful and bright. Tricky details from the text were illustrated with well-selected images.

A few minutes later, I was overwhelmed. While each individual sentence went down fine, the cumulative effect wore on me. There was an example I couldn’t make sense of, and then a whole section that as a student I might not have understood at all.

I wish I could tell you that there’s a science of textbook design. As far as I can tell, there is not. What we have instead is psychological research that can help us think more clearly about design choices.

One common problem of direct instruction is that it can leave students not thinking deeply enough about the content. What happens instead could be called surface-level comprehension, or even shallow information processing.
Try remembering a seven-digit number while also reading Twelfth Night. You’ll likely feel overwhelmed: that’s too much ‘cognitive load’, and it harms your thinking and learning.
A textbook can’t be a great book – it needs to be a great teacher. We should look towards teaching research for inspiration on how to design excellent, learnable texts.
